response.title: how to power a mobile dog grooming van
response.answer:
To power a mobile dog grooming van, you have four main options: a gas generator, a lithium battery system, the van's engine, or shore power (plugging into an external outlet).

For a professional grooming van, I would recommend a hybrid battery + generator setup or a sufficiently large lithium battery system if you want quiet operation.

1. What equipment needs power?

A typical mobile dog grooming van needs electricity for:

Equipment

	

Typical power consumption




High-velocity dog dryer

	

1,200–2,400 W




Electric water heater

	

1,200–1,500 W




Air conditioner

	

800–1,800 W




Grooming clippers

	

20–60 W




Water pump

	

50–150 W




Electric grooming table

	

200–500 W (intermittent)




LED lighting

	

20–60 W




Ventilation fan

	

30–100 W

The biggest power consumers are usually the dog dryer, water heater, and air conditioner.

For example, if you're running:

Dog dryer: 1,800 W

Air conditioner: 1,200 W

Water pump and lighting: 150 W

Your total power requirement is approximately 3,150 watts.

If the electric water heater turns on at the same time, that could increase to 4,650 watts.

This is why many professional grooming vans need a system capable of delivering roughly 4,000–6,000 watts, depending on the equipment and which appliances can run simultaneously.

2. Four ways to power your grooming van
Shop

Option A: Gasoline generator

Lowest initial cost

A 5–7 kW generator can run most grooming equipment. It requires fuel, regular maintenance, safe outdoor exhaust routing, and noise management.

Estimated equipment cost: $1,000–$4,000+

Shop

Option B: Lithium battery + inverter

Quiet operation

Uses a large lithium battery bank and a 5–6 kW inverter. No generator exhaust while operating. Battery capacity and charging speed determine how many dogs you can groom per day.

Estimated installed cost: $8,000–$20,000+

Shop

Option C: Engine-powered charging

A high-output secondary alternator charges your auxiliary batteries while driving or idling. This reduces dependence on a separate generator but requires compatible vehicle hardware and sufficient charging capacity.

Estimated cost: $3,000–$8,000+, depending on the battery system.

Shop

Option D: Shore power

Plug into a properly rated 120 V or 240 V electrical connection at a home or commercial location. Excellent for overnight battery charging, but less convenient when working at customers' homes.

Estimated hardware cost: $200–$1,000+, excluding electrical installation.

3. How big a battery do you need?

The battery size depends on how many dogs you groom daily and whether you use electric water heating and air conditioning.

Here is an illustrative estimate for a van operating for 8 hours:

After accounting for inverter losses and a reserve, you might want a 15–18 kWh lithium battery bank for this workload.

Assumes 80% of nominal battery capacity is available for AC loads after losses and reserve. Actual loads vary by equipment and climate.
4. My recommended setup

For a full-time mobile dog grooming business, I would consider:

5–6 kW pure sine wave inverter with adequate surge capacity.

10–20 kWh LiFePO4 battery bank, depending on daily usage.

Secondary alternator or DC-DC charging while driving.

Shore power for overnight charging.

Optional generator as backup for long days.

Have a qualified RV or vehicle electrical installer design the system, including battery protection, properly sized wiring, breakers, grounding, ventilation, and safe generator exhaust. Never operate a portable generator inside the van or an enclosed compartment.
